items.question: Why did you find the panelists’ predictions about AGI and job creation confusing?
items.object: Predictions about AGI and job creation at a panel on AI's future
items.answer: The moderator asked at the very beginning of the panel whether we thought it was more likely than not that by 2030 we would get AGI, defined as AIs that can do everything humans can do. Seven or eight hands went up, not including mine because my timelines are somewhat longer than that. But then he asked a follow-up question a couple questions later about whether we thought that AI would create more jobs or destroy more jobs over the following 10 years. So, 2030 was five years, and seven out of 10 people thought that we would have AGI by 2030, but then it turned out that eight out of 10 people, not including me, thought that AI would create more jobs than it destroyed over the next 10 years. I was a little confused. I was like, why is it that you think we will have AI that can do absolutely everything that the best human experts can do in five years, but will actually end up creating more jobs than it destroys in the following 10 years? What's happening here?

items.question: How do you think venture capitalists’ use of the term AGI shapes their expectations about its impact?
items.object: Venture capitalists’ use of the term AGI
items.answer: When I poked some people later in the panel about that seeming tension, they really quickly backed off and said, you know, what does AGI really mean? The moderator had defined it as this very extreme thing. But they were like, you know, we kind of already have AGI. People keep moving the goalpost. We keep making cool new products and people aren't accepting that it's AGI, and they aspire to something higher. I thought that was funny because, in the old-school singularitarian futurist definition, AGI is this very extreme thing. But I think VCs have an instinct to call something AGI that is like GPT-5 is AGI, or something just much milder. So I think this creates a situation where people feel like they've gotten a lot of evidence that AGI isn't a very big deal and doesn't change much because we already have AGI or we're going to have it next year or we got it two years ago and, you know, look around us, nothing much is changing.

items.question: How do you expect AI to change the world by 2050?
items.object: AI-driven technological change by 2050
items.answer: I feel like there's this expectation where, whether or not we get AGI in the next few years, a lot of people are starting to not really care about that question. They still expect the next 25 years and the next 50 years to play out kind of like the last 25 years or the last 50 years, where there's a lot of technological change between 2000 and 2025, but it's a moderate amount of change. They kind of expect that in 2050, there will be a similar amount of change as there was between 2000 and 2025, even if they think that we're going to get AGI in 2030. They think AGI is just what's going to drive that sort of continued mild improvement. Whereas I think that there's a pretty good chance that by 2050, the world will look as different from today as today does from the hunter-gatherer era. It's 10,000 years of progress rather than 25 years of progress driven by AI automating all intellectual activity.

items.question: How do you understand the spectrum of views about how radically AI could change the world in the coming decades?
items.object: The spectrum of views about AI-driven technological change in the coming decades
items.answer:
Yeah, so I would say on the standard mainstream view, if you ask a normal person on the street what 2050 will look like, or if you ask a standard mainstream economist, I think they would think, well, the population is a little bit bigger. We have somewhat better technologies. Maybe they have a few pet technologies that they're most interested in, and maybe we have this one or that one. Slightly better medicine. People live slightly longer. And yeah, it's an amount of change that's extremely manageable.

I think on the far extreme from there, on the other side, is a view described in If Anyone Builds It Everyone Dies, wherein that worldview, at some point, probably pretty unpredictably, we crack the code to extreme superintelligence. We invent a technology that rather suddenly goes from being like GPT-5 and GPT-6 and so on to being so much smarter than us that we're like cats or mice or ants compared to this thing's intelligence. Then that thing can immediately have really extreme impacts on the physical world. The classical, canonical example here being inventing nanotechnology: the ability to precisely manufacture things that are really tiny and can replicate themselves really quickly and can do all sorts of things, and inventing space probes close to the speed of light and things like that.

I think there's a whole spectrum in between, where people think that we are going to get to a world where we have technologies approaching their physical limits. We have spaceships approaching the speed of light, and we have self-replicating entities that replicate as quickly as bacteria while also doing useful things for us. But we're going to have to go through intermediate stages before getting there. Something that unites all of the people who are AI futurists and concerned about AI x-risk is that they think in the coming decades we're likely to get this level of extreme technological progress driven by AI.

items.question: How do you understand the disagreement between AI accelerationists and people worried about AI existential risk over how fast AI should develop?
items.object: AI accelerationists’ and existential-risk advocates’ expectations about the pace of AI development
items.answer: I've found often that reasonable people who are AI accelerationists tend to think that the default course of how AI is developed and deployed in the world is very, very, very slow and gradual. They think that we should cut some red tape to make it go at a little bit more of a reasonable pace. People who are worried about x-risk think that the default course of AI is this extremely explosive thing where it overturns society on all dimensions at once in maybe a year or maybe five years or maybe six months or maybe a week. They're saying, oh, we should slow it down to take 10 years, maybe. Meanwhile, the accelerationists think that by default diffusing and capturing the benefits of AI will take 50 years or 100 years, and they want to speed it up to take 35 years.

items.question: How do you expect the arrival of AI that outperforms top human experts at computer-based work to change the pace of automation?
items.object: Top-human-expert-dominating AI and the automation of physical work
items.answer:
I think that probably in the early 2030s, we are going to see what Ryan Greenblatt calls top human expert dominating AI, which is an AI system that can do tasks that you can do remotely from a computer better than any human expert. So it's better at remote virology tasks than the best virologist, better at remote software engineering tasks than the best software engineers, and so on for all the different domains. By that time, I feel like probably the world has already accelerated and changed, and narrower and weaker AI systems have already penetrated in a bunch of places, and we're looking at a pretty different world. But at that point, I think things can go much faster, because I think top-human-expert-dominating AIs in the cognitive domain could probably use human physical labor to build robotic physical actuators for themselves. That would be one of the things that, whether the AIs have already taken over and are acting on their own or humans are still in control of the AIs, I think that would be a goal they would have of automating the physical as well.

I think I have pretty wide uncertainty on exactly how hard that'll be. But whenever I check in on the field of robotics, I actually feel like robotics is progressing pretty quickly and it's taking off for the same reasons that cognitive AI is taking off. Large models, lots of data, imitation, large scale is helping robotics a lot. So I imagine that you can pretty quickly, maybe within a year, maybe within a couple years, get to the point where these superhuman AIs are controlling a bunch of physical actuators that allow them to close the loop of making more of themselves, doing all the work required to run the factories that print out the chips that then run the AIs, doing all the repair work on that, and gathering the raw materials.

items.question: How do you understand the outside view that leads people to expect AI to produce relatively slow economic change?
items.object: The outside view behind expectations that AI will produce slow economic change
items.answer: I feel like at the end of the day, the different parties tend to lean on two different, pretty simple priors or simple outside views. The party that expects things to be a lot slower tends to lean on: for the last 100, 150 years in frontier economies, we've seen 2% growth. Think of the technological change that has occurred over the last 100 or 150 years. We went from having very little, electricity was just an idea, to everywhere being electrified. We had the washing machine, the television, the radio, all these things happened; computers happened in this period of time. None of these show up as an uptick in economic growth. There's this stylized fact that mainstream economists really like to cite, which is that new technology is the engine that sustains 2% growth, and in the absence of that new technology, growth would have slowed. This is how new technologies always are. People think that they're going to lead to a productivity boom, but you never see them in the statistics. You didn't see the radio, the television, the computer, the internet, and you're not going to see AI. AI might be really cool; it might be the next thing that lets us keep chugging along. That's one perspective. It's an outside view they keep returning to. And also just a somewhat more generalized thing, which is things are just always hard and slow, way harder and slower than you think.

items.question: How do you understand the case for AI driving economic growth much faster than 2% per year?
items.object: The historical and feedback-loop case for AI accelerating economic growth
items.answer:
I think the alternative perspective leans a lot on much longer-term economic history. If you attempt to assign reasonable GDP measures to the last 10,000 years of human history, you see acceleration. The growth rate was not always 2% per year at the frontier. 2% per year is actually blisteringly fast compared to what it was in 3000 BC, which is maybe 0.1% per year. So the growth rate has already multiplied many-fold, maybe an order of magnitude, maybe two. People in the slower camp tend to feel like the exercise of doing long-run historical data is too fraught to rely upon. But people in both camps do agree that the Industrial Revolution happened, and the Industrial Revolution accelerated growth rates a lot. We went from having growth rates well below 1% to having 2% a year growth rates.

People in the faster camp tend to lean on the long run and on models that say that the reason we had accelerating growth in the long run was a feedback loop where more people can try out more ideas and discover more innovations, which leads to food production being more efficient, which leads to a larger supportable population, and then you can rinse and repeat, and you get super-exponential population growth. That perspective says that AIs, if you can slot in AIs to replace not just the cognitive, but the cognitive and the physical, the entire package, and close the full loop of AIs doing everything needed to make more AIs, or AIs and robots doing everything needed to make more AIs and robots, then there's no reason to think that 2% is some sort of physical law of the universe. They can grow as fast as their physical constraints allow them to grow, which are not necessarily the same as the constraints that keep human-driven growth at 2%. So that's the justification that they provide for their perspective in broad strokes.

items.question: Why do you think people who expect slower AI-driven growth remain unconvinced by arguments for much faster growth?
items.object: The worldview of people who expect slower AI-driven growth
items.answer:
I'm honestly not sure. I think maybe one part of it is that I'm partial to the things-will-be-crazier side of things, so I'm not sure I'll be able to give a perfectly balanced account. One thing I've noticed on the side of people who think it'll be slower is that their worldview kind of has a built-in error theory of people who think things will go faster. Their worldview is not just things will keep ticking along, but everyone thinks there will always be some big new revolution that makes things—everyone's always expecting it to speed up, and they've always been wrong. So there's that dynamic, which is, from their point of view, totally reasonable. Even if there isn't some knock-down argument in the terms of your interlocutor where you can point to a mistake that they'll accept, or even if you look at the story and think it's plausible, you still have this strong prior that someone could have made the same argument about television, someone could have made the same argument about computers. None of these played out.

I think there hasn't been that much dialogue, and there could be more, including dialogue that is trying to ground things in near-term observations. But I think that's a big part of it. They have an error theory built in that makes the object-level conversation about how the AI could make the robots and the robots could bootstrap into more robots not feel very legitimate or interesting. They sort of have a story where that type of thinking always leads to a bias toward expecting things to go faster than they actually will because it's hard for that kind of thinking to account for all the drag factors and all the bottlenecks.

items.question: How do you understand the stakes of the disagreement over whether bottlenecks will limit AI-driven economic growth?
items.object: Bottleneck objections to rapid AI-driven growth and the stakes of resolving the disagreement
items.answer: I think people who think things will go faster feel like everyone is always blanket assuming that there are going to be bottlenecks. They bring up specific bottlenecks, and those specific bottlenecks, when you look into them, don't seem like reasons to think that 2% is where the ceiling is, or even that 10% is where the ceiling is. items.question: How do you think we should measure whether AI is speeding up software development and AI R&D?
items.object: Empirical evidence of AI speeding up software development and AI R&D
items.answer: One thing that I think will not address all of this, but is a step in the right direction, is really characterizing how and why and if AI is speeding up software and AI R&D. METR came out with an uplift RCT, which I think was the first of its kind, or at least the largest and highest quality, where they had software developers split into two groups. One group was allowed to use AI, the other group was disallowed from using AI, and they studied how quickly those developers solved issues, tasks on their to-do list. items.question: How would you change AI companies' benchmark reporting to make it more useful for tracking emerging risks?
items.object: Reporting internal AI capability benchmark results
items.answer:
I think there's a whole spectrum of evidence about AI capabilities where, on the one hand, the easiest to test but least informative is benchmark results. Companies do release benchmark results when they release models right now. They'll say Claude Opus 4 was released and have a model card that says it has this score on a hacking benchmark, this score on the software engineering benchmark, and so on as part of a report about whether it's dangerous. GPT-5 had the same thing. I think that's great that they do that, but in my ideal world they would release their highest internal benchmark score at some calendar-time cadence. Every three months they would say they've achieved this level score on a hacking benchmark, this level score on a software engineering benchmark, and this score on an autonomy benchmark. Danger could manifest from purely internal deployment, because if they have an AI agent sufficiently good at AI R&D, they could use that to go much faster internally, and then other capabilities and therefore other risks might come online much faster than people were previously expecting. So it's not ideal to have your report card for the model come out when you release it to the public, unless there's some sort of guarantee that you're not sitting on a product substantially more powerful than the public product.

Maybe it's fine to release your model card and system card along with the product if you also separately have a guarantee that you won't have too much of a gap between the internal and the external. That's how I would tweak information that's currently reported to be somewhat more helpful for this concern.

items.question: Why do you think information relevant to AI safety should be open to public scrutiny rather than handled by a small government body?
items.object: Public scrutiny of information relevant to AI safety
items.answer:
We're building the plane of AI safety research as we're flying it. It's not a box-checking exercise that any kind of government agency that's often understaffed, especially with technical staff, could do. We want this information out in the open, and then we want people to do involved analyses of it. Our sense of what information we even want is probably going to be shifting over time, and it'll probably go better if there's a robust external scientific conversation about what indicators we want to see, what that would mean, and when we should trigger alarm. If that's all routed through governments with 10 or even 50 people who have to deal with it, it'd be very hard for them to interpret the evidence quickly and well enough, be confident enough to sound the alarm, and have people actually listen to them. If I imagine sounding the alarm on something like the intelligence explosion, I picture it having to be a society-wide conversation, kind of like sounding the alarm about COVID.

Something I have in mind is when Joe Biden had that disastrous debate performance that led to weeks of conversation that ultimately led to him being removed from the ticket. It would have been hard for a small, narrow group of people entrusted with the authority to make the same thing happen.

items.question: How do you assess the idea of using early transformative AI systems to manage the risks from more advanced AI?
items.object: Using early transformative AI to manage the risks of more advanced AI
items.answer:
The opportunity that's created is that we have a lot more AI labor and much smarter potential researchers than we did before. So why don't we turn that new resource toward solving this problem that at the moment we don't really know how to fix? I think some people who are not too worried about AI look at society as a whole or history and say, "Well, technology has enabled us to do all kinds of more destructive things, but we don't particularly feel like we're in a more precarious situation now or at much greater personal risk now than in 1900 or in 1800, because advances in destructive technology have been offset by advances in safety-increasing technology. On balance, probably things have gotten safer." The idea is, well, can we potentially pull off the same trick in this crunch time period?

A lot of people who are more concerned about AI risk are very dismissive of this plan. It sounds like a plan that's really flying by the seat of your pants, expecting the thing that's creating the problem to solve the problem. But humanity has repeatedly used general-purpose technologies that both created problems and solved those problems. Automobiles created the opportunity for carjackings and drive-by shootings, and empowered bad actors in various ways. But if the police and law enforcement have cars as well, that is a balance. When you imagine a future with some crazy new advanced technology and imagine all the problems it creates, it can be hard to imagine, with the same level of detail and fidelity, all the responses to those problems that are also enabled by that technology. You could imagine someone worrying about the rise of fast vehicles and neglecting to think about how the ways they cause bad things could be kept in check by people using vehicles for law enforcement and similar.

Similarly with computers, you can hack things with computers, but computers also enable you to do a lot of automated monitoring for that kind of hack and automated vulnerability detection. You couldn't imagine a police force not using computers. I think the basic principle is sound: if you're worried about problems created by technology, one of the first things on your mind should be how you can use that new technology to solve those problems. You're not imagining cars creating broad-based rapid acceleration of all sorts of new technologies and potentially just a 12-month window or two-year window or six-year window before everything goes totally crazy. It's important not to blow through that window, to monitor as we're approaching it and how long we have. items.question: How do you assess whether using early transformative AIs for alignment research is more vulnerable to misalignment than using them for other work to protect civilization?
items.object: Misalignment risks in using early transformative AI for alignment research and other protective work
items.answer: I do think misalignment, the prospect that these early AIs, these early transformative AIs are misaligned, is a huge obstacle to this plan that needs to be shored up and handled and specifically addressed. I don't think that it necessarily bites harder for getting the AIs to do alignment research than for getting the AIs to do anything else helpful, because if they have it out for you, they don't necessarily want to help you shore up your civilization's defenses. If you're imagining trying to get a hardened misaligned AI to help you with biodefense, if it's misaligned and, for example, wants the option of threatening you with a bioweapon in its arsenal in the future, it would similarly have an incentive to do a bad job at that as it would to do a bad job at alignment research. In general, I think there's one big concern, which is whether the AIs that we're trying to use at that point in time will have motivations that give them incentives to undermine the work we're trying to get them to do. They certainly would have incentives to undermine alignment research if they were misaligned, but I think they would also have incentives to undermine efforts to make ourselves more rational and thoughtful.

items.question: How do you think confidence in solving AI alignment affects the appeal of using AI to solve alignment and other problems?

items.answer: I think the distinction I was drawing is for people who thought that the alignment problem was extremely hard to solve and we were way off track to solving it. items.question: Which problems do you see as priorities for advanced AI to help us solve during an intelligence explosion?
items.object: Using advanced AI to address alignment and strengthen societal defenses
items.answer: One obvious one is just AI alignment. That is the foundation of everything else. But then there are also other things that are not really about AIs at all, just broad societal defenses. items.question: How do you view Forethought's grand challenges as potential uses of AGI labor during crunch time?
items.object: Forethought's grand challenges as potential applications of AGI labor during crunch time
items.answer: I interviewed Will MacAskill and Tom Davidson from Forethought earlier in the year. The organization has a long list of what they call grand challenges, which they suspect are probably amenable to this kind of AGI labor during crunch time. Other ones are ensuring that society doesn't end up locked into particular values prematurely, which cuts off our ability for further reflection and changing our mind; the potential use of AI or AGI, insofar as it's very steerable and follows instructions, in power grabs by the people operating it; and space governance. If we start to be able to use resources in space, how would we share them? How would we divide them such that there's not conflict ahead of time, because people anticipate that once you start grabbing resources in space, you're on track to become overwhelmingly dominant? There's epistemic disruption. I guess new competitive pressures, concerns that you can end up in a sort of Malthusian situation if you have competition between many different AIs, and possibly some others that are missing here. We don't know which of these are going to loom large at the time. Some might feel like they've been addressed, or perhaps that we were hallucinating issues that aren't so severe. But there are many different ways that we could potentially apply it.

items.question: What do you see as the necessary conditions for using AI to help make future AI systems safe?
items.object: Using AI to help make future AI systems safe
items.answer: Fundamentally, I think you need there to exist a window of opportunity where, before AIs are uncontrollably powerful or have created unacceptable levels of risk, they are really capable and really change the game for AI safety research. items.object: The intelligence explosion as a crunch time for AI-powered research
items.answer:
You might just think if AI can help us do research or work to solve any of these problems, then as soon as it's able to do that, we want to do it, whether or not an intelligence explosion is kicking off. To some extent that's right. I think the reason I focus so much on the intelligence explosion is twofold. One is because at that point I think we might have a pretty short clock to figure out a bunch of stuff. The default trajectory might look like 12 months to extremely powerful, uncontrollable superintelligence that can easily take over the world. So it changes our calculus: you might want to focus on very short-term things rather than things that have long lead times, at least at crunch time if not before. The other thing is I think crunch time can help alleviate some of the challenges we've been talking about with AIs not being good at the full spectrum of things we want them to be good at, because by definition at that point AIs are really good at further AI R&D.

One of the things we could do with AIs that are good at AI R&D, at least in most cases, is try to direct their AI R&D toward filling out the skill profile of AIs and getting them to be good at some of the types of things we want them to be good at that they aren't so good at right now. At that point you might have much more capability at your disposal, and it might be much more worth putting in the effort to fine-tune and scaffold and do all these other things to make your AI that's good at moral philosophy or your AI that's good at biodefense.

items.question: How do you think about using pauses in AI development to give us time for protective work during an intelligence explosion?
items.object: Pausing and redirecting AI development during an intelligence explosion
items.answer:
I think of it as making the pause less binary. If you think of the default path as almost 100% of AI labor going into further rounds of making AIs better and making more AIs and more chips, and you think of a pause or a stop as 0% of the world's AI labor going toward those activities, I think there's a whole spectrum between 0 and 100%. Then I think of it as answering the question of what you do in the pause: you do all this protective stuff, and you have these AIs around to do it with. Once you have that frame of making the pause less binary and thinking really hard about what you do during a pause, you might often end up thinking it's worth going a little bit further with AI capabilities, because especially if we tilt the capabilities in a certain direction, we might at the end of that get AIs that are much better than they are right now at biodefense while still not being uncontrollable or that scary. You can imagine a bunch of little pauses and little redirections during that whole period.

I would hope that at some point in the period we do activities like policy coordination that cause us to have longer in this sweet spot of AIs that are powerful enough to help with a lot of stuff but not so powerful that we've already lost the game.

items.question: How would you want society to navigate the transition from AI R&D automation to vastly superhuman AI if a clear early warning sign indicated an intelligence explosion was approaching?
items.object: Slowing the transition from AI R&D automation to vastly superhuman AI
items.answer: If a really clear early warning sign triggers that we are about to enter into this intelligence explosion, fast takeoff space, where we go in the space of 12 months from AI R&D automation to vastly superhuman AI, then I would vote for shifting that trajectory to be 10 times longer or even longer than that, and trying to make that transition as a society in 10 years instead of one year, or 20 years instead of one year. I still wouldn't advocate for pausing and then hanging out for 10 years and then unpausing, because I think slowly inching our way up is better than pause, then unpause and have a jump. But I think the frame of using AIs to solve our problems applies regardless of whether you're white-knuckling it in one year, eking out an extra two months, or manage to get the consensus and common knowledge that allows the world to step through it in 10 years.

items.question: Why do you think AI companies' plans to use AI for technical alignment are most likely to fail?
items.object: AI companies' plans to use AI for technical alignment
items.answer:
If it fails, it's probably most likely to fail because they just didn't actually do a big redirection from using AIs for further AI capabilities to putting a lot of energy toward using them for AI safety. They say this is their plan, but they don't really have quantitative claims about what fraction of their AI labor or their human labor at that stage is going to go toward safety versus further acceleration. They'll be facing tremendous pressure from their competitors to stay ahead. My guess is that unless they have much more robust commitments than they have right now, they probably just won't be directing that much of their AI labor. If they have 100,000 really smart human equivalents, maybe only 100 of them are working on AI safety, which is maybe still more than they had before in human labor, but not that much compared to how quickly things are going.

Other mechanisms would be that it's legally required, the government basically insists that most of the compute go toward this, or at least that most of it is not going toward recursive self-improvement. Or the companies could reach some sort of agreement where they say we'd all like to spend more of our compute on this kind of thing, so we're going to have some contract where we're going to spend 50% of all of our compute and not lose relative position in particular.

items.question: How do you think efforts to use AI for alignment and safety work are most likely to fail?
items.object: Failure modes of using AI to help with alignment and safety
items.answer:
The most likely way it fails is that they don't go super hard on it. But it's also plausible that they're just trying to get the AIs to help with alignment, and the AIs are misaligned and the control procedures and other things are ineffective, so they deliberately only help with further AI R&D and don't help with alignment and safety and biodefense and all these other things you'd want them to help with. I would hope that at that stage the transparency regime is strong enough that that fact is broadcast really widely, and then that could inspire a change in policy that causes us to slow down. But in that world it's a bad world, even if we do slow down a lot, because we're on our own. We have to do this stuff without the AIs' help because we can't get them to help us. But I'm reasonably bullish about control techniques getting early AIs that are not super galaxy-brain superintelligences to be helpful for a range of stuff that they're good at.

Another way that they could end up not making that much of an effort is if the window is relatively brief and it just takes a long time to get projects off the ground.

items.question: How do you think Open Philanthropy should prepare to make AI-powered work a major part of its grantmaking as an intelligence explosion approaches?
items.object: Open Philanthropy’s preparation for AI-powered research and an intelligence explosion
items.answer:
For now, the biggest thing we need to do is very similar to the biggest thing I think society needs to do to prepare for the intelligence explosion, which is track where we're at right now in terms of how useful AIs are for the work that we do and the work our grantees do. Push ourselves to automate ourselves and push our grantees to automate themselves, and track how good AI is at the stuff Forethought does, the stuff Redwood Research or Apollo does, and the stuff our policy grantees do. One thing is socializing within ourselves: "Hey, it's probably a big deal when the AIs start to get really good at any good thing we're funding. And once we start to see signs of life there, we should be prepared to potentially go really big on that."

Crunch time isn't 100% a special thing. We absolutely shouldn't wait until crunch time to do anything at all. It's just the prediction that crunch time is the point when a lot of things that were hard to automate before become easier to automate. If it turns out, for example, that AI is really good at math research, which I think is plausible, then maybe we should deliberately shift our technical grantmaking toward more mathy kinds of technical grantmaking, because that's an area where you can churn a lot more; it's so much more tractable. Having a function that's looking out for these things and poking OpenPhil and its grantees to consider shifting their work toward more easily automatable things, and repeatedly testing whether their work can be automated, is a big thing. I could imagine down the line having separate accounting for the rest of our grantmaking versus grantmaking that is going toward paying for AIs for our grantees.

We already pay for ChatGPT Pro subscriptions and ChatGPT API credits for tons of grantees. I think just making it more salient in our minds—what fraction of our giving is going toward that, do we endorse its size, is there any place we should be going bigger, are we on track, is the percentage climbing the way we think it should be, does that seem in line with the way AI capabilities are climbing? If we think crunch time is going to start in six years, are we on track to have inference compute be a large fraction of our spending at that time? Psychologically, I could imagine if I was leading Open Philanthropy, or one of the donors being advised, and we did have these transparency requirements and did start getting a sense that an intelligence explosion might be kicking off, I could imagine dithering for a long time.

items.question: Why do you think Open Philanthropy might need a different decision-making process to spend a billion dollars on highly automatable work?
items.object: Open Philanthropy's grantmaking process for large investments in automatable work
items.answer: I think this is a very natural institutional concern. Even beyond being scared of making a mistake on this front, organizations have particular ways they do things and processes. Right now OpenPhil's grantmaking process looks like someone fairly junior gets an opportunity across their desk, either through an open call or some contact they have, and that junior person pulls together materials to convince their manager it's a good fit. Then that manager convinces someone higher up, and you can have two, three, or sometimes four layers of information cascading up the decision-making process before it's approved. If the right thing to do is spend a billion dollars on some particular strain of work that's super automatable, that isn't something you'd trust some random junior person to make that call. You might need a different process for that. I don't know what that process would look like, but I think that would be one thing to figure out.

items.question: How do you think uneven AI capabilities could affect OpenPhil’s readiness to invest heavily in crunch-time AI labor?
items.object: OpenPhil’s readiness to invest heavily in crunch-time AI labor
items.answer: I think there are two possibilities here. One possibility is that by the time it's the right move to dump a bunch of money on crunch-time AI labor, OpenPhil itself has already been largely automated. That's an easy world, because we have a visceral sense that AIs are really helpful: maybe we've slowed down junior hiring, all our program associates are AIs, and we're totally transformed as an organization. The evidence and conviction to pull the trigger might be easier to achieve, and we have a bunch of labor. Maybe we have a thousand people on the AI team instead of the 45 we have now. They can figure all this stuff out much more quickly. The concerning possibility is jaggedness: maybe AI is extremely good at math and technical AI safety and certain specific kinds of manufacturing useful for a PPE play, but we haven't automated ourselves. It's not that good at doing our jobs, because there wasn't much of that stuff in the training data. We're just not set up to absorb AI labor. It makes horrible mistakes in a way that you can catch in software or manufacturing, but on the OpenPhil side it's harder; you need humans to do that. So we're not very automated and don't have a visceral sense that it's time now, that AIs are really good and we have to go big. But it would still be the right thing to do to pour a bunch of money into AI labor on these few heavily automated verticals.

items.question: How do you think about the challenges an external group faces in securing enough AI labor during an intelligence explosion?
items.object: External groups’ access to AI labor during an intelligence explosion
items.answer:
I see two challenges to getting access to enough labor as an external group. One is whether they'll even sell to you. In AI 2027 and a lot of stories of the intelligence explosion, you get to a point where one company has pulled far enough ahead of its competitors that it keeps its best internal systems to itself and only releases systems considerably worse than its internal frontier, just good enough to be ahead of its competitors' released products. There can be a growing gap in how intelligent the best internal systems are and how intelligent the best externally accessible systems are.

items.question: How do you think an intelligence explosion could change competition among AI companies and access to their models?
items.object: Competition and access to AI during an intelligence explosion
items.answer: It describes the present day, and that's a change from a few years ago, when I do think OpenAI had way more of a lead and it seemed more plausible that there would be a monopoly or duopoly. But there are reasons to push in the other direction: if you have a super-exponential feedback loop, you have a bunch of actors growing at an increasingly rapid rate, first at 2%, then 4%, then 8%, and they don't interact with one another, you do get a winner-take-all dynamic. If they're growing on the same growth curve but one gets to a particular milestone first, that leader gets more and more powerful and wealthy relative to the laggards. items.question: How do you think competitive pressure shapes whether a leading AI company keeps its capabilities secret?
items.object: A leading AI company's incentives to keep its capabilities secret
items.answer: I think it depends a lot on the competition landscape they face. If the other companies are really far behind, there's a pretty strong incentive and reason to keep your capabilities secret, because you give up quarterly profits, but maybe you don't care about that because you're running on investment money anyway. If you can get your AI to help you make better AI to help you make better AI and so on, you could emerge with superintelligence that might give you power that rivals nation states or the ability to decisively control how the future goes. That might be very attractive to a power-seeking company. It does involve forgoing short-term profits, though, which means that if competitors are close at your heels and your investors are breathing down your neck to deliver quarterly earnings, you can't tell your investors, "Don't worry, we have a superintelligence," because then that will get out. And your plan is to screw over the investors in this case. Your plan is to create a superintelligence, not to pay them back. Create a superintelligence and take over the world, maybe. They won't like that. There's a mismatch in incentives between the investors and the CEO, and the CEO is being a bad agent to their principal. The more things look like an efficient competitive market with very little slack, the more the leading company will be forced to provide access to the rest of us.

items.question: How do you assess AI companies’ incentives to devote AI labor to addressing societal risks?
items.object: AI companies’ incentives to use AI labor to address societal risks
items.answer:
I think it's unclear. Certainly they have some incentive to be into this. But the two alternative uses of AI labor that might be more attractive to them are, one, power-seeking for themselves: building up an enormous AI lead over everyone else, then bursting onto the scene with an incredible amount of power and the ability to challenge the US government or nation states. That might be attractive to some people. I think that would be a very evil strategy to pursue, but it's definitely in the water. The other thing is more mundane: using these AIs to make normal goods and services, the products, media content, and other services that people most want to pay money for in the short term. It's very similar to how right now we don't spend a huge fraction of society's GDP on biodefense, cyber defense, and moral philosophy. That's not what people want to pay for. AI is a thing that accelerates the creation of products and services people want to pay for, and this isn't very high on the list.

Most people are not looking to become dictator of the world or take on huge amounts of power, but the kinds of people who end up leading very risky technology projects are somewhat more ambitious than the typical. So I suppose we can't rule that out as a possibility.

items.question: How do you think we should prioritize work now to prepare for future AIs that can understand the situation and solve problems faster than we can?

items.question: What did you want from OpenPhil’s technical AI safety grantmaking strategy that you felt was missing?
items.object: OpenPhil’s technical AI safety grantmaking strategy
items.answer:
I was focused on grants to technical researchers. These were often academics, sometimes AI safety nonprofits, working on interpretability or some kind of adversarial robustness. They seemed like reasonable research bets, but I felt unsatisfied, and I think this is going to be a theme of my career. I felt unsatisfied that the theory of change hadn't really been grounded out and spelled out: how would this type of interpretability research lead to this type of technique or ability we have, and how could that fit into a plan to prevent AI takeover in this way? Similarly for any of the other research streams we were funding. This had been the big thing that deterred me from getting involved in OpenPhil's technical AI safety grantmaking for a long time, even though I was one of the few people on staff who thought about technical AI safety outside of that team.

Most grant decisions in the 2015 to 2022 period turned on heuristics: this person's a cool researcher and they care about AI safety. That's totally reasonable, but I wanted more of a story for how this line of research addressed a critical problem, why we thought it was plausibly likely to succeed, and what it would mean if it succeeded. We never had that kind of built-out strategy because it's very hard and a lot to invest in. Having been thrown headfirst into grantmaking with the FTX crisis, I thought maybe I wanted to take on the AI safety grantmaking portfolio, which at the time didn't have a leader because all the people who'd worked on it had left, some to go to the FTX Foundation.

items.question: How did you approach grantmaking when you took responsibility for a program area at OpenPhil?
items.object: A barbell strategy for grantmaking at OpenPhil
items.answer:
I ended up pursuing a compromise. One thing that comes with the territory of this role is that there have been grantees we made grants to in the past that are up for renewal, and part of the responsibility of being the person in charge of this program area is to investigate those renewals and decide whether we should keep the grantees on. I tried to follow what an OpenPhil canonical decision-making process would be for those grants. I tried a barbell strategy: for renewals, I wouldn't hold myself to the standard of understanding and defending the proposal on the technical merits, but would lean more on heuristics: this person seems aligned with the goal of reducing AI takeover risk, this person has a broadly good research track record, and so on, and try to make those grants relatively quickly.

But I would also develop a different funding program, or grants I really wanted to bet on, where I would try to hold myself to that standard and write down why I thought it was a good thing to pursue. The second thing turned into making a bet, in late 2023 to mid-2024, on AI agent capability benchmarks and other ways of gaining evidence about AI's impact on the world. items.question: Why did you find it difficult to run an AI safety grantmaking program without close intellectual engagement from your organization's leadership?

items.answer:

When he left, leadership was more stretched thin, and the people who remained didn't have as much context and fluency with all this AI stuff as Holden did. I wrote up a big memo saying we should do AI safety grantmaking in a more understanding-oriented way, develop inside views, and explaining why I thought that would be good. items.question: What drew you to effective altruism as a way of thinking about helping the world?
items.object: Effective altruism as an approach to helping the world
items.answer:
I'll open with what it is: a movement or idea that you should think explicitly, seriously, and quantitatively about how you can do the most good with your career or money that you're donating, and that different career paths and charities you could donate to could differ by orders of magnitude in how much good they do. If you're working on reducing climate change, it could be orders of magnitude more helpful to research green technologies than to get people to turn off their lights or conserve electricity in their personal use. There's an ethos that if you're taking this seriously and really care about helping the world, you stop and think and do the math. In the same way that if you had cancer, or your spouse had cancer, you'd do the research and figure out what treatments had what side effects and success rates and ask the doctor a lot of questions.

There's an ethos that that's what it looks like when you take something seriously. A lot of people doing good in the world do what makes them instinctively feel good. There's another approach where you respect the intellectual depth of the problem. I was really drawn to this. I fell headfirst into the EA rabbit hole when I was 13, so it's been more than half my life that I've been extremely involved in this community and way of thinking. There were maybe three big things I really liked about this approach. One is that EAs challenge themselves to care about people and beings very different from them, far away in time and space. Even the most "vanilla" EA cause area of global poverty: the vast majority of money given by individuals in rich countries to alleviate poverty goes to helping other individuals in rich countries, even though money could go much further overseas in countries where people have a much lower standard of living. People donate locally because they feel more affinity for people closer to them and more similar to them. EA also has strains that challenge people to extend care to animals, future generations thousands or millions of years in the future, and artificial intelligence, if it can be conscious and feel pain. That was really appealing to me.

There was also a way of going about doing things that appealed to me: they were nerdy and intellectual, thinking things through and methodologically innovating on how to figure out which charities are better. There were interesting arguments. They were transparent, with a culture of open debate and admitting mistakes. GiveWell, an early pillar of the EA movement, had a mistakes page on its website where it discussed mistakes it had made. They were honest and high-integrity in a way that doesn't obviously follow from caring about other beings more. For example, GiveWell refused to do donation matching because donation matching is usually a scam, where the big donor would have given that much anyway even if you hadn't made your donation. That whole package was really attractive to me. It hit a lot of psychological buttons at once and felt like my people and the way I wanted to live my life.

items.question: How do you assess the analogy between effective altruism and religious movements?
items.object: The analogy between effective altruism and religious movements
items.answer: I think EA aspires to be and very much succeeds in being more truth-seeking than the world's religions and a lot of other communities and movements. In that sense there's an extremely important disanalogy. But it's not a bad analogy in some ways, because for people deeply involved in the EA community, it provides a map of the good life, a vision of what it means to be good and have a good life. It's unlike a political movement in that it doesn't just have a set of policy prescriptions, but like many religious movements it intersects with politics. People might approach political questions, like whether to ban gestation crates for pigs, through their commitment to EA. It's not just a community or social club. People get solace and friendship from their local community of EAs like they do from a local church community, but it's more than that. It tries to say something about the sweep of the world and your place in it, and what it means to live a good and meaningful life, while intersecting with politics and community without being exactly the same.

items.question: Why do you think it's a mistake to define effective altruism by the particular causes its professional communities pursue?
items.object: Effective altruism as a way of thinking about the good
items.answer: I don't think that's really what EA is. It's a mistake to collapse EA into a set of three or four goals in the world, like reducing suffering of animals in factory farms, improving quality of life for poor people in developing countries, and AI safety. People think of EA as a weird umbrella for those three things, which are professional communities pursuing well-defined goals. But EA is more a way of looking at the world and thinking about the good. You can take an EA approach to cause areas more parochial than the big three: US policy, from the perspective of the welfare of US citizens, doing rigorous cost-effectiveness analysis of what policies help and don't help. A lot of people do. EA can also generate new cause areas to add to the canon. There's fertile ground for whether EA could help society prepare for radical change by advanced AI. AI safety is one big important thing, but there might be a range of other issues, which you might prioritize based on your values and sense of how things will play out.

items.question: Why would you personally have liked the effective altruism community to have more of a spiritual role in your life?
items.object: The effective altruism community’s professional structure and potential spiritual role
items.answer: I'm someone who really benefits from structure and emotional motivation reinforcement. I also tend to socially conform a little, or try to achieve the ideal of the community I'm in. The ideal of my corner of the EA community is to have a really impactful job, do a really good job at it, and work a lot of hours. That's the message you get from the community, and that's what I try to do. I personally would have liked more of a spiritual angle. If you read my colleague Joe Carlsmith's blog, I get some of that existential reflection about our morality and values, and the crazy thing so many EAs believe: that in a decade or two we might be in an utterly transformed world, utopic or dystopic relative to this vantage point. items.question: What do you think effective altruism contributes to thinking about AI disruption?
items.object: Effective altruism's distinctive contribution to thinking about AI disruption
items.answer: I think EA thinking and values probably still have a lot to add in the age of AI disruption. EAs will mostly be the ones thinking seriously about whether AIs themselves are moral patients, whether they should have protections and rights, and how to navigate that thoughtfully against tradeoffs with safety and other goals. EAs will also take most seriously the possibility that AI disruption could be so disruptive that we end up locked into certain societal values, gaining the technological ability to shape the future for millions or billions of years, and thinking about how that should go. There are degrees of extremity to the AI worldview. Even if you accept that AI will disrupt everything in the next 10 or 20 years, the people thinking hardest about the most intense disruptions will be disproportionately EAs, because EA thinking challenges you to engage in far-seeing, rigorous speculation, even though it's hard to know the future. EAs try hardest to peek ahead anyway.

items.question: What do you think characterizes effective altruism organizations’ approach to questions that resist rigorous measurement?
items.object: Effective altruism organizations’ willingness to make explicit judgments under uncertainty
items.answer: Even the tamest EA cause areas, like global health and development, have a huge dose of this. GiveWell's cost-effectiveness analysis has to grapple with the value of doubling someone's income when they make very little, compared with a certain risk of death, or the value of a painful disease. They try to get answers from surveys and weird studies people have done. It's not very rigorous in the end, and they have to form and spell out their judgments. I think the willingness to tackle questions like this and say, "Here's our answer," even though there's a lot to argue with, is emblematic of EA organizations, including the best AI safety EA organizations like Redwood Research.

items.question: How do you think effective altruists who are comfortable tackling speculative questions should contribute to the world’s response to major changes like AI?
items.object: Effective altruism’s role in responding to major changes like AI
items.answer: For people with that mindset, they should take advantage of having this unique or reasonably rare mentality and go into roles other people probably won't fill because they feel too uncomfortable or think it's misguided.
